summary: SARPulse is a free, no-login web app that lets anyone see and hear the Earth move using NASA-ISRO NISAR radar. Optical satellites can’t see through clouds, darkness or treetops, and can’t detect millimetres of motion. Radar can. SARPulse streams live NISAR L-band and NASA OPERA radar imagery from NASA GIBS and pairs it with interferograms you control: switch between four radar bands from four space agencies and watch the fringes and noise change. It also turns ground motion into sound, where sinking lowers the pitch and every fringe clicks. We focus on our home, Miami: 35 coastal high-rises that sank 2 to 8 cm (2016 to 2023), and Everglades water moving under the sawgrass, part of a ~$23B restoration plan. We label every layer LIVE, MODEL or MEASURED, handle Surfside honestly, and present radar as a screening tool for inspectors and water managers, never a collapse predictor. Earth has a pulse. Now you can see it and hear it.
details:
Earth has a pulse. Normally only radar can detect it, but with SARPulse, anyone can see and hear it, even in clouds, night and the trees.

Optical satellites require daylight and clear skies, are stopped at the canopy and are unable to detect millimetres of movement. Radar, however, can measure the echo’s phase. Take two passes over the same ground: any change in phase is motion toward or away from the satellite, where displacement = (λ/4π) Δφ. Half a wavelength of ground motion is one full colour cycle, or fringe. This is 11.9 cm for NISAR L-band, 4.7 cm for NISAR S-band, 2.8 cm for Sentinel-1 C-band and 11.8 cm for SAOCOM L-band. SARPulse turns this physics into something people can play with. They can scrub through time, switch bands to view fringes multiply and noise grow, compare to an optical photo over the Everglades, and listen. Ground motion sets the pitch: sinking glides toward 55 Hz and rising climbs toward 440 Hz, with one click per fringe, plus hiss from low coherence. This demonstrates that when one changes from L to C band, about four times more rings are heard and seen, which explains the importance of wavelength.

It was constructed around our home. In 2024, an InSAR study revealed that 35 coastal high-rises in Miami (Sunny Isles to Miami Beach) subsided 2–8 cm from 2016 to 2023. The Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan has an estimated $23 billion price tag and relies primarily on water flowing under sawgrass, which a camera wouldn’t even see. L-band radar can detect water-level change under that canopy at ~15 cm per fringe, every 12 days. We also added Iceland’s Svartsengi volcano, Thwaites Glacier and the Amazon, as any location is just a bounding box away.

We were deliberate about what is real. Each of the layers in the app has a tag:

LIVE: NISAR L-band GCOV, OPERA RTC-S1 backscatter and OPERA DSWx-S1 radar water maps, streamed at view time from NASA GIBS.

MODEL: the interferograms, computed in the browser from physics models (Mogi volcanic source, tidal flexure, construction creep, wetland double bounce) calibrated to published studies. They are not processed NISAR interferograms; they teach how InSAR works. A 12-day pair at Miami’s speeds is mostly atmosphere, and slow motion requires a multi-year time series.

MEASURED (optional): real OPERA DISP-S1 velocities for Miami Beach, pulled by our Python pipeline with a free Earthdata login.

INFO: context (with sources) without a data layer.

The physics is unit tested as well. On wetlands our code gives 14.9 cm per fringe, in line with the published 15 cm per fringe from FIU. Every published number in the app is tied to a citation on screen, and our own design choices, such as the triage tiers, are labelled as proposals.

The same care shaped how we frame safety. InSAR found no settlement at Champlain Towers South before the 2021 collapse, and NIST’s findings point to a structural punching-shear failure, so we use radar as a screening tool, not a collapse predictor. Our plan is to use NISAR’s L-band to detect motion, rank areas by the speed of movement, and hand that list to people before a failure rather than after. The triage levels (under 1, 1 to 2.5, over 2.5 mm per year) are a proposal for discussion, not an engineering standard, and individual buildings are not named. We hope the app will be used by inspectors and condo boards to determine which barrier-island buildings to inspect first in conjunction with Florida’s SB 4-D milestone inspections, to provide Everglades managers with a view of water change under the canopy, and to allow students and the public to play around with radar science, enjoy it and learn.

Next, we plan to ingest NISAR’s own time series (GUNW, DISP-NI), provide measured velocities for all the buildings in Miami, use ascending and descending passes to separate vertical from east-west motion, validate Everglades water against USGS EDEN gauges, and send alerts in English, Spanish and Haitian Creole. We also plan to develop a physics-informed neural network (PINN) trained on SAR time series such as OPERA DISP-S1 and NISAR products. Instead of learning from data alone, the network would be constrained by the same equations the app already uses: the line-of-sight projection, the creep law s(t) = v₀τ(1 − e^(−t/τ)), and the wetland and volcanic source models. This would allow it to distinguish true movement from atmospheric noise, fill gaps between passes, and predict the trend of each area within a range of uncertainty. The aim is quicker and more accurate triage and prediction: rankings based on cleaner, physically consistent velocities in many more locations, with minimal manual calibration, which would extend our reach well beyond Miami. Its outputs would be labelled MODEL on screen like every other modelled layer and would be validated against held out passes and, for Everglades water, USGS EDEN gauges. It would focus the human engineer’s first look and would not supplant inspection.

Built using Next.js, React and strict TypeScript and hosted on Firebase, SARPulse is a simple, installable web app. It does not require any logins, API keys or special hardware, just a phone or laptop browser, and it was developed and tested on regular laptop computers. It features a 3D globe over OpenFreeMap vector tiles, rendered by MapLibre GL. Interferograms are drawn in a Web Worker using OffscreenCanvas, so each frame costs only a few multiply-adds per pixel, and sound is played using the Web Audio API. The measured-data pipeline is Python with earthaccess. The home-page globe flight is pre-rendered with Playwright so it loads quickly, and Vitest, ESLint and pytest back the code with 55 TypeScript and 6 Python tests. The app is accessible by design, with keyboard controls, ARIA labelling, reduced-motion support and sound to convey the same information a second way, and there is an offline basemap in case the venue’s Wi-Fi fails. The whole project is open source (MIT).

We used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding and research assistant. It verified our assertions, contributed much of the code and tests, and produced documentation. We selected the challenge and the focus on Miami, determined what the app should contain, tested every feature, and can explain the physics. AI was not used to generate or alter any NASA logos or flags.
